title: Watch and pray (Luke 21:29–38)
hookLine: don't let your hearts be weighed down with cares; watch and pray

lines: THEN, A FIG TREE IN LEAF.
ELEVEN AT NIGHT, MIND STILL RUNNING.
cards: Jesus has been saying hard things about the end: wars, signs, Jerusalem surrounded by armies. His closing words aren't about armies at all.
They're about a fig tree in leaf, and the weight a person carries all day and takes to bed at night. The unanswered email. The bill.
The thing a sister said at dinner. Eleven at night, the day is over, and the mind is still running. His warning reads as if it were written for that hour.

teach.h: THE FIG TREE: SUMMER IS NEAR.
teach.b: First the tree. When the fig tree and all the trees put out leaves, you know summer is near. Nobody needs a calendar; you just look.

teach.h: MY WORDS SHALL NOT PASS AWAY.
teach.b: Then a sentence about what lasts: "Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away."

And the warning, in the King James words: "Take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares."
Overcharged: the Greek means weighed down, made heavy. Three things on the list. Surfeiting: the Greek word is used for the heavy head after a night of drinking, something close to a hangover.
Drunkenness. And cares of this life: ordinary worries. He puts worry on the same list as a hangover; both leave the heart too heavy to notice what's coming.
Then the cure: "Watch ye therefore, and pray always."

teach.h: STAY AWAKE, LIKE A NIGHT GUARD.
teach.b: The Greek for watch means to stay awake, like a guard on night duty. Not anxious. Alert.
Luke ends the chapter with Jesus living it out.

teach.h: WATCH YE THEREFORE, AND PRAY ALWAYS.
teach.b: By day he teaches in the temple. Every night he goes out to spend the night on the Mount of Olives. Early every morning, the people come to hear him.
Not a slogan for a crisis, but a rhythm: carry the day lightly enough that you can still see the leaves.

how: Some Christians keep an evening prayer, such as Compline, to hand over the day before sleep, and some churches read this chapter in the season of Advent.

o: the heavy head after too much drink
too much sleep, a lazy kind of rest
a sudden flood that drowns the fields

games.q: what's inside Luke 21:29–38 — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus lists worry alongside drunkenness and its hangover
surfeiting, drunkenness and cares of this life: all three weigh the heart down.
'watch' here means stay anxious and on edge
the word means stay awake, like a guard on night duty: alert, not frantic.
Luke says people came early in the morning to hear Jesus in the temple
by day he taught in the temple; at night he lodged on the Mount of Olives.

games.q: Jesus has warned of hard days ahead. what does he say is most likely to make people miss the day when it comes?
o: not studying the signs closely enough.
hearts weighed down with excess and the cares of this life.
games.why: "lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life." ordinary heaviness, not a lack of information.

practice: Notice what's sitting heaviest on you today and name it plainly, in a few words.

Imagine it as an actual weight in your hands, and without solving anything, set it down for tonight on the floor beside the bed; it will still be there in the morning if you need it. If you pray, hand it to God by name.

wordCard.voice: Surfeiting, the heavy, hungover feeling Jesus warns can weigh a heart down, along with drunkenness and ordinary cares.

orig.note: Greek: stay awake, keep from sleeping. the word Luke uses for 'watch' in 21:36.

carryVoice: Your line: carry the day lightly enough. The fig tree is already in leaf. That's day five hundred seventy-six.
